claims.text: Elevated-temperature Cr–Zr interdiffusion is responsible for premature failure of elemental Cr coatings on zirconium-alloy cladding.
An Al2O3 interlayer will significantly suppress high-temperature Cr–Zr interdiffusion.
The Al2O3 interlayer will preserve protective performance during normal subcritical-water operation.
The Al2O3 interlayer will preserve protective performance during accident-relevant high-temperature steam exposure.
An Al2O3 layer on the order of tens of nanometers is an appropriate diffusion-barrier thickness.
Approximately 300°C represents the normal subcritical-water operating condition relevant to the hypothesis.
Normal-operation performance must be sustained over durations of years.
Approximately 900°C steam represents the accident-relevant high-temperature condition considered by the hypothesis.
The relevant accident exposure duration ranges from minutes to hours.
A continuous nanoscale Al2O3 layer physically separates the Cr coating from the Zr-alloy substrate.
Physical separation by the Al2O3 layer inhibits atomic diffusion between Cr and Zr.
Al2O3 acts as an inert and stable diffusion barrier under the proposed normal and accident conditions.
Impeded Cr–Zr exchange prevents formation of deleterious intermetallic compounds.
Preventing Cr–Zr interdiffusion and intermetallic formation maintains Cr-coating integrity under normal and transient high-temperature conditions.
Relative to the unmodified Cr-coated baseline, the barrier-modified system will have a thinner interdiffused layer after accident-relevant exposure.
Relative to the unmodified baseline, the barrier-modified system will form fewer or no Cr–Zr intermetallic phases.
The barrier-modified system will provide protective performance during normal subcritical-water operation similar to that of the unmodified Cr-coated baseline.
Unmodified Cr-coated zirconium alloy undergoes accelerated Cr–Zr interdiffusion around 900°C.
Accelerated Cr–Zr interdiffusion around 900°C leads to premature failure of the unmodified coating.
